prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of stability and accuracy

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B041) with Katori and Ye as my final position. Nothing in round 1 weakened the core case and several points strengthened it. The scientific idea is single and sharply defined: trapping neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength, where the lattice light shift cancels for the clock transition, gives many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation. That is what made stability and systematic uncertainty at the 1e-18 level reachable, and independent laboratories now agree at that level and compare clocks across continents, so maturity is established by measurement and not by anticipation. The consequences are physics results: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tighter limits on drifts of constants, ultralight dark-matter searches. The chair asks for wording that anchors the citation on the lattice clock itself. I propose exactly that: the citation names the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock as the invention, and mentions the comb and ion control of 2005 and 2012 by neither name nor claim, so that it cannot read as a third precision-spectroscopy prize. On Ye, I accept Kroll's and Pearce's concern that part of his reputation rests on comb-based spectroscopy, but the credit I am assigning rests on what is distinctly his group's: the strontium lattice clock taken to record accuracy and stability, and the many-body, spin-polarised Fermi-gas clock physics that exposed and controlled collisional and light-shift systematics. That is lattice-clock work and does not depend on the comb. I did not change my preferred configuration from round 1; what changed is that I am now more explicit about the citation boundary and about why topological insulators, which I regard as conceptually deeper, remain an alternative and not my lead.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is that this honours a measurement invention in territory already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and that it asks less of our picture of nature than topological or moire matter. I judge that the first part is met by the citation wording above, because the lattice concept is neither a frequency comb nor single-ion control. The second part is a genuine difference in conceptual reach and I do not dismiss it, but the prize covers inventions and the downstream physics here is concrete. A second weakness is that two names leave out Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups, whose contributions to specific accuracy milestones are real; the supplied credit allows only the pair, and I regard them as the originating concept and the decisive demonstration of the many-atom regime. The redefinition of the second has not happened, but I do not think the prize should depend on that decision.

responses.point: The lattice concept itself, not combs or ion traps, is the citable discovery, and the citation should be restricted to it; Ye's credit is the open question.
responses.response: I agree, and I have written my citation on that basis. On the chair's question about Ye, I think his claim is well grounded in the lattice clock: record strontium lattice accuracy and stability, and the many-body clock work. I would not rest his credit on the comb. Your Boulder stay in Hall's laboratory is a proper disclosure, but it does not seem to me to require recusal given that you report no collaboration with either laureate; the committee should simply note it, as the chair suggests, and I would not want it to weaken your scientific argument, which I find sound.

responses.point: He wants the question of how much of Ye's credit rests on the lattice clock settled before the final ballot, and he keeps IceCube as a first alternative while conceding the credit is the weak point.
responses.response: I think the question can be settled on the evidence supplied: the citation names the lattice clock, and what is credited to Ye is the realisation of lattice-clock accuracy and many-body clock physics. If the committee instead wanted to honour the comb-based spectroscopy, that would be the 2005 prize again, so the wording should exclude it. On IceCube, I respect your instrumentalist concern about a two-person split and I share it: I do not think the maturity of source identification, with one blazar at about three sigma and NGC 1068, supports a prize this year, even though the diffuse flux is secure.

responses.point: She asks whether the prize would be more natural after the SI redefinition of the second, and notes that many Sr and Yb groups are not among the credited names; she also dropped Mele from her view of the topological insulator credit.
responses.response: On timing I still disagree, and I note your own later comment that the pending redefinition cuts in favour of the prize and not against it. I accept that a many-group field makes any narrow credit imperfect, and that is why I want the citation tied to the originating concept and its decisive realisation. On topological insulators, your point that Kane and Mele are a single theoretical step is what I accepted in round 1 when I moved to the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio. I still keep that as my first alternative, though the BHZ and 3D allocation problem makes me place it behind the clocks.

responses.point: She ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for its field-creating effect and concedes that she cannot claim B017 is safer than B041 on maturity or attribution; she also names the Chalmers tie to me.
responses.response: I agree with your own assessment that B041 is the safer prize on maturity and attribution, and I find the field-creating argument for B017 a real one. My difference is that the superconducting mechanism and sample variability are still unsettled, which for me tips the balance toward the clocks this year, while I keep B017 as an alternative for a later year when the moire picture is firmer. On the Chalmers tie you mention, I confirm that I and you are colleagues at the same university and have no documented collaboration; it should not matter for B041, which is far from our own fields.

responses.point: He asks the committee to say plainly whether it wants a metrology invention, and he proposes that the citation name the lattice clock explicitly and that the many-groups point is the strongest objection to narrow credit.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should say plainly that it is choosing an invention with physics consequences, and I would not hide it behind discovery language. My answer to the invention-versus-discovery question is to apply the same criterion to every candidate and not asymmetrically: the Nobel statutes cover both, and the lattice clock has produced measured physics, such as the redshift over millimetres. I accept your point on the many-groups objection and resolve it as you do, by anchoring on the lattice concept and its record-setting realisation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the boundary against the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or would prefer a wider clock citation that adds other laboratories; the three-person limit and the supplied credit constrain that choice.

Whether Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley or the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups have claims that the pair cannot cover; I rely on the supplied credit and on recollection of priority, which I have not independently verified.
Whether the committee prefers to await the SI redefinition of the second; I think not, but I cannot rule out that colleagues weigh it differently.
For B004, the allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Hasan remains contestable and I have not independently verified 3D priority.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B041: I have no documented connection to Katori or Ye. For B004 and B017 I have no documented tie either. I repeat that for circuit QED (B028), which no member prefers, I work in the field with Chalmers colleagues and would recuse from that candidate. I note Olsson's mention of our shared Chalmers affiliation, with no documented collaboration. Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize, which is not relevant to the preferred configuration. I see no recusal need arising from Kroll's disclosure.
